recommendations.title: Your specifics are stranded in paragraphs
recommendations.summary: Several specification-shaped facts — figures with units, labelled values — sit inside prose rather than in a list or table. Moving them into a definition list or table makes them survive summarising.
recommendations.rationale: This is not the same as having no lists at all, which is already checked. It is that the facts most worth citing are the ones still in prose. When a summariser condenses a long page it drops sentences before it drops table rows, so a specification in a paragraph is the first thing to disappear and the exact thing a user was asking for.
recommendations.evidence: 10 specification-shaped facts sit in paragraphs against 5 in lists or tables, e.g. '99.999%'
recommendations.snippet:
{{FACT_LABEL}}{{FACT_VALUE}}
{{FACT_LABEL_2}}{{FACT_VALUE_2}}
recommendations.validation: Read your page and list every number a customer would ask about. Confirm each one now appears in a table row or definition list, not only inside a sentence.

recommendations.title: Your claims carry no date and no source
recommendations.summary: This page states figures but gives no publication date and cites nothing. Adding a visible date and naming where a figure comes from raises how much weight a retrieval system gives it.
recommendations.rationale: Extractability and credibility are different problems, and only the first is normally measured. A retrieval system that can read a claim perfectly well will still discount it when nothing says when it was true or who established it, because an undated figure cannot be checked for staleness. Sites optimise hard for the first and almost never for the second.
recommendations.evidence: 64 numeric claims on the page, with no <time> element, no datePublished and no citation
recommendations.snippet:

{{CLAIM_SENTENCE}} {{SOURCE_NAME}}
recommendations.validation: Confirm the page shows a date a reader can see, and that it is inside a `<time datetime=…>` element or a `dateModified` field. For each headline figure, confirm a reader can tell where it came from.
